abstract.p: Because interactions among microbial growth kinetics, biofilm formation, hydrodynamic conditions, and mass transfer constraints frequently limit process stability and scale-up, the simultaneous removal of chemical oxygen demand (COD) and nitrate from wastewater remains a significant challenge in biological treatment systems. The hydrodynamic and mass transfer characteristics of a Draft Tube Spouted Bed Bioreactor (DTSBBR) were examined for the simultaneous removal of chemical oxygen demand (COD) and nitrate from synthetic wastewater under different operating parameters. In a biofilm-assisted reactor, performance was assessed at dilution rates (0.6, 0.9, and 1.2/h) and granular activated carbon (GAC) loads (10, 20, and 30 g). The biofilm thickness, substrate diffusion, external mass transfer coefficient, Reynolds number (Re), Schmidt number (Sc), and Sherwood number (Sh) were precisely studied and evaluated under the influence of reactor hydrodynamic studies. The COD elimination confirmed higher mass transfer capability compared to the nitrate values because of diffusion-limited denitrification kinetics, with Sherwood numbers ranging from 4.60 to 7.10 and mass transfer coefficients between 0.66*10–6 and 1.04*10–6 m/s. The empirical correlations Sh = 0.86 Re 0.52 Sc 0.33 for COD and Sh = 0.76 Re 0.50 Sc 0.33 for nitrate were obtained by diffusion-controlled substrate transport and substantial hydrodynamic dependence. The Monod kinetic experiments showed µmax values of 0.25/h for COD and 0.23/h for nitrate, with a constant Ks of 25 mg/L for COD and 14 mg/L for nitrate. The obtained results confirmed that DTSBBR provided consistent simultaneous organic and nitrogen removal, enhanced biofilm activity, and efficient substrate transport, demonstrating its applicability for advanced biological wastewater treatment applications.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: The need for effective wastewater treatment solutions has led to an increasing demand for research on biological reactor systems that can simultaneously remove organic carbon and nitrogenous contaminants. Chemical oxygen demand (COD) and nitrate, two of the most important pollutants affecting aquatic ecosystems, are frequently found in high amounts in wastewater produced from industrial, agricultural, and municipal sources1,2. High COD levels in water bodies reduce DO, degrading the ecosystem and reducing aquatic biodiversity; similarly, high nitrate levels cause groundwater pollution, eutrophication and public health issues like methemoglobinemia3. Hence, an effective treatment system to remove COD and nitrate simultaneously is to be developed.

Today, attached growth reactors have drawn a lot of attention and interest compared to other treatment systems, due to their high hydraulic shock loads, high biomass concentrations and greater treatment efficiency4. Among such available bioreactors, Spouted bed bioreactors in particular have become attractive alternatives to conventional activated sludge and fixed-bed systems due to their enhanced mixing properties, reduced clogging tendencies, improved oxygen and nutrient transfer, and high biomass retention capacity5,6. The performance of the reactor is further enhanced by the addition of a draft tube, which increases internal circulation patterns, particle movement and fluid distribution. These developed draft tube spouted bed bioreactors (DTSBBRs) combine the advantages of fluidised bed and biofilm reactors to optimise substrate contact.

Hydrodynamic behaviour parameters like liquid circulation, particle motion, turbulence intensity, mixing efficiency, and biofilm formation significantly influence the biological reactor’s performance7. The rate of biodegradation influences substrate transport from the bulk liquid phase to the biofilm surface. Treatment efficiency, in addition to microbial activity, is determined by the rate at which substrates permeate through the liquid boundary layer and into the biofilm matrix. To optimise reactor operation and provide reliable scale-up criteria, there is a need to understand and study the hydrodynamic and mass transport properties of the reactor.

The simultaneous removal of COD and nitrate is very much influenced by mass transfer. The substrates drift from the bulk liquid to the biofilm surface via an external liquid film and then diffuse into the microbial layer where biological reactions take place. Reactor performance is affected if substrate movement is obstructed. These mass transport and hydrodynamic conditions are linked and described by dimensionless quantities such as the Reynolds number (Re), Sherwood number (Sh), and Schmidt number (Sc)8. The Reynolds number signifies hydrodynamic flow regions and mixing concentration; the Sherwood number quantifies the efficiency of mass transfer, and the momentum and molecular diffusion are characterised by the Schmidt number9. These empirical relations, with dimensionless numbers grouped, are used in the optimisation and scaling up of the reactor design.

The kinetic analysis of the reactor, in addition to hydrodynamics and mass transport studies, helps in understanding the microbial growth behaviour and substrate utilisation mechanisms10. Mathematical models that describe microbial growth and substrate consumption well depict reactor performance. Such biological wastewater treatment systems are well defined by the Monod kinetic model11. The two parameters that influence the microbial growth rate through Monod models are the maximal specific growth rate and the half-saturation constant, with accurate kinetic coefficients evaluated to design large treatment systems12.

The mass transfer and hydrodynamics in fluidised and spouted bed reactors are studied by many researchers13,14. An increase in particle circulation, in turn increasing turbulence, has created higher external mass transfer coefficients and restricted diffusion in the biofilm. The bioreactor employing granular activated carbon (GAC) as a support medium has shown higher pollutant removal efficiency, as there is greater biomass attachment and also due to the combined effect of adsorption and biodegradation15. Although research has been done on the biological removal of organic carbon and nitrogen using attached-growth reactors, few integrated studies examine reactor hydrodynamics, biofilm formation, microbial growth kinetics, and external mass transfer in Draft Tube Spouted Bed Bioreactors simultaneously. Specifically, there is a dearth of quantitative data on the Monod kinetic parameters, biofilm efficacy, Thiele modulus, external mass transfer coefficients, and empirical Sherwood–Reynolds–Schmidt correlations needed for reactor design and scale-up. To improve the practical application of DTSBBR for continuous wastewater treatment and build predictive design tools, these information gaps must be filled.

Considering all the above points, the present study investigates biodegradation kinetics and hydrodynamic studies for simultaneous removal of COD and nitrate using a Draft Tube Spouted Bed Bioreactor (DTSBBR). The reactor has been studied by evaluating various parameters like concentrations, GAC loading and dilution rate. The reactor behaviour has been quantified by evaluating external mass transfer coefficients, the Thiele modulus and dimensionless numbers such as Schmidt, Sherwood and Reynolds. Monod kinetics have been studied by evaluating the kinetic growth characteristics. The potential of the DTSBBR has been studied for its sustainability and effectiveness in the simultaneous removal of COD and nitrate from wastewater.

sec.title: Microorganism
sec.p: A mixed microbial consortium was obtained from local sewage wastewater samples, which were precisely mixed to obtain a representative microbial population capable of concurrently digesting nitrate and organic carbon. Approximately 2.5 L of the mixed wastewater was improved in a lab environment after being transferred to a culture medium. To promote microbial growth and acclimatization, one liter of a synthetic nutritional medium containing dextrose (370–695 mg/L) as the carbon source, potassium nitrate (460 mg/L) as the nitrogen source, magnesium sulphate (10 mg/L), ferrous sulphate (0.08 mg/L), potassium dihydrogen phosphate (2.5 mg/L), and calcium chloride (1.8 mg/L) was prepared in known concentrations and added to the culture.

Over the course of a 144-hour enrichment period, the nutrient medium was refilled every 48 h to guarantee adequate nutrient availability and promote the growth of active heterotrophic and denitrifying bacteria. Granular activated carbon (GAC) particles were added to the culture medium to aid in microbial immobilisation after the surplus liquid phase was properly decanted after the enrichment period. Because of their large specific surface area, porous structure, and advantageous surface characteristics for microbial attachment, the GAC particles functioned as a support matrix for biofilm formation.

To ensure adequate microbial colonisation and the formation of an initial biofilm layer, the injected GAC particles were kept in a static environment for an extra 48 h. Microorganisms clung to the activated carbon surface throughout this time, forming permanent biofilm colonies that could use nitrate and organic carbon as substrates. The biofilm-coated GAC particles were recovered and utilised as the biological carrier material in the Draft Tube Spouted Bed Bioreactor (DTSBBR) studies following successful immobilisation.

sec.title: Assay of Nitrate and biomass
sec.p: At numerous times, samples were taken from the draft tube spouted bed reactor and examined for a variety of traits. COD and Nitrate were measured using the Online Water Analyzer, Tethys Instruments Model: UV500-C, after the culture samples were spun at 10,000 rpm for 10 min (REMI, India). The weight difference of the attached biomass was measured before and after the solids were cleaned with a 0.25 N NaOH solution and dried for 24 h at 105 °C. The scanning electron microscope (SEM) was used to measure the thickness of the biofilm as per the procedure explained in Joshi et al., 202131. Rui’s empirical relation was used to compute the biofilm dry density16.

sec.title: Bioreactor experimentation
sec.p: The 3” cylindrical column with a 1” PVC centre draft tube makes up the DTSBBR experimental setup. The reactor had a 1.4-litre capacity. A brass conical bottom is attached to the cylindrical column. The column’s core body is flanged, with a conical section at the bottom and a top section that houses the outlet. To keep the draft tube in place, two guides are flanged at the top and bottom of the column. Two separate inlets allow air and artificial water to enter the column from the bottom of the cone. The solid medium is granular activated carbon. Water from a 10-litre feed tank is continuously supplied to the column by a peristaltic pump. The 1 HP compressor provides the air directly. To prevent solid particle carryover, two filters smaller than 0.5 mm are installed at the intake and output. Figure 1 depicts the DTSBBR experimental setup and spouting circumstances. The reactor was run for different initial nitrate (50, 100, 150 and 200 mg/L) and COD (100, 200, 300 and 400 mg/L) concentrations, different GAC loadings (10, 20 and 30 g) and different dilution rates (0.6, 0.9 and 1.2/h). Figure 2 depicts the materials and methodology of the whole process carried out.

sec.title: Modelling studies
sec.p: The external mass transfer characteristics during simultaneous removal of COD and nitrate in the spouted bed reactor were investigated using dimensionless analysis involving Reynolds number (Re), Schmidt number (Sc), and Sherwood number (Sh). The studies were carried out at different dilution rates (0.6, 0.9, and 1.2/h) and GAC loadings (10, 20, and 30 g). The obtained values of biofilm thickness, Thiele modulus, effectiveness factor, observed reaction rate, and external mass transfer coefficient were used to develop empirical mass transfer correlations for COD and nitrate removal. Based on the experimental results, the following parameters were used to calculate the values, as presented and discussed in the results section.

sec.title: Biofilm thickness
sec.p: During bed operation, the biomass concentration increases on the supporting media, which increases the volume of the bioparticle. The thickness of the bioparticle before and after running the reactor was examined by SEM analysis.

sec.title: Mass transfer correlations
Effect of initial COD and nitrate concentration on time at different dilution rates to attain steady state
sec.p: The time required to achieve steady-state operation in biofilm-based reactors is a significant performance indicator because it establishes the adaptability of microorganisms, the stable growth of biofilms, and the balancing of substrate loading and biodegradation capacity. Figure 3 (a) and 3 (b) illustrates the effect of COD and nitrate concentrations respectively in the Draft Tube Spouted Bed Bioreactor (DTSBBR) on the time required to achieve steady-state conditions at different dilution rates (/h) and GAC loadings (g). The results demonstrate that when the starting substrate concentration increased, the steady-state time increased for both COD and nitrate removal. The reactor attained steady-state conditions for COD elimination in 8–15 h at an initial dosage of 100 mg/L, while it took roughly 30–40 h at 400 mg/L as shown in Fig. 3 (a). Similarly, steady-state was obtained after 10–20 h at 50 mg/L of nitrate and 25–40 h at 200 mg/L as shown in Fig. 3 (b). The stabilisation time lengthens with greater substrate concentrations because the microbial population is exposed to more organic and nitrogen loading. Microbial growth, enzyme induction, and the development of a metabolically active biofilm that can hold the increased substrate flux at higher substrate concentrations all require longer acclimation durations17. In fluidised-bed and moving-bed biofilm reactors, it has been demonstrated that higher influent concentrations prolong the biofilm adaptation period and delay the attainment of stable operating conditions18.

The effect of GAC loading significantly reduced the time required to achieve steady-state conditions. The reactor constantly reached steady-state faster at 30 g GAC loading than at 20 g and 10 g GAC loadings for all substrate concentrations investigated. For example, with 30 g GAC loading, steady-state was reached at 400 mg/L COD in roughly 30–35 h, but at 10 g GAC loading, it took 35–40 h as shown in Fig. 3 (a). Nitrate removal exhibited a similar trend as shown in Fig. 3 (b). The higher specific surface area available for microbial adhesion and biofilm formation enhanced effectiveness at larger GAC loadings19.

The biomass retention increases and accelerates the stabilising process due to a larger active microbial population and enhanced substrate consumption capacity. Also, the activated carbon increases microbial adaptability and hence decreases substrate shock loadings by adsorbing organic molecules. Similar results of GAC-supported biofilm reactors showed that enhanced mass transfer and biomass immobilisation have accelerated the steady-state conditions20.

At the lower dilution rates, microorganisms efficiently removed the pollutants because of the consistent metabolic activity due to prolonged hydraulic retention time and enhanced substrate biofilm interaction. However, at higher dilution rates, greater substrate concentration increases hydrodynamic stress and loading rate and extends the required time to attain steady state. The configuration of the draft tube spouted bed reactor enhances substrate dispersion with better recirculation of liquid and enhances particle mobility, hence reducing the concentration gradients throughout the reactor. Similar hydrodynamic advantages have been demonstrated at higher circulation rates, with improved biomass-substrate interactions in fluidised bed and spouted bed reactors21. It’s observed that DTSBBR demonstrated hydrodynamics in which the biofilm support medium and substrate concentration interact to regulate the steady state. The reactor configuration not only enhanced mixing and substrate transport, but also enhanced steady-state operation across a range of operating conditions.

Improved microbial attachment on the activated carbon surface, increased resistance to biomass washout, and improved substrate distribution due to continuous particle circulation within the draft-tube spouted bed reactor are responsible for the shortest start-up period and stable simultaneous COD and nitrate removal among the operating conditions examined. The improved mixing characteristics reduced concentration gradients around the biofilm and enabled faster microbial adaptation to the influent wastewater. On the other hand, raising the influent COD and nitrate concentrations increased the microbial consortium’s substrate loading, necessitating more time for biomass acclimatisation and biofilm maturation before steady degradation rates could be established. However, the current findings show that by carefully choosing the carrier loads and hydraulic working conditions, this effect can be greatly reduced. Thus, this study’s engineering significance is not in verifying the anticipated impact of substrate concentration, but rather in showing how reactor hydrodynamics and biofilm support media optimisation can significantly shorten reactor start-up times without sacrificing treatment effectiveness.

sec.title: Kinetic studies for COD and nitrate reduction

caption.p: Monod kinetic studies for COD and nitrate reduction.

sec.p: It is observed from Fig. 4 that COD removal was higher with the highest specific growth rate (µmax) of 0.25/h, with Ks being 25 mg/L, indicating rapid microbial growth and effective organic substrate biodegradation. The main component of COD is biodegradable organic matter, which provides heterotrophic bacteria with a direct source of carbon and energy. As a result, the microbial consortia inside the biofilm demonstrated increased substrate consumption efficiency and quicker growth kinetics. The obtained µmax value shows that the reactor maintained active biomass growth under different substrate concentrations and had strong biological oxidation capabilities. Similar ranges of µmax for COD biodegradation in biofilm reactors were observed18,24, where heterotrophic growth rates in connected growth systems typically ranged between 0.2 and 0.6/h.

Microorganisms’ attraction for the organic substrate is reflected in the observed Ks for COD, which was determined to be 25 mg/L. Lower Ks values often indicate stronger substrate affinity, while higher values suggest that higher substrate concentrations are needed to reach half of the maximum growth rate25. The study’s intermediate Ks value indicates that the microbial population maintained a fairly high affinity for the COD substrate while still requiring a sufficient substrate concentration for long-term development. This behaviour is common in biofilm-based systems where extra resistance to microbial uptake is contributed by substrate diffusion through the biofilm layer26. The COD kinetic constants show the balanced substrate conditions without significant inhibitory effects.

The nitrate Monod kinetics showed a lower Ks of 14 mg/L and a maximum specific growth rate µmax of 0.23/h. Denitrification proceeded at a slower biological rate than organic oxidation, as confirmed by the somewhat lower µmax compared to COD. Nitrate reduction to nitrite, nitric oxide, nitrous oxide, and ultimately nitrogen gas in anoxic circumstances is the multi-step biochemical reduction process known as denitrification27. Denitrifying microorganisms typically have slower growth kinetics than heterotrophic COD-degrading bacteria because of these successive enzymatic processes28. Thus, the decreased growth rate observed in the nitrate environment confirms the comparatively slower denitrification process occurring within the biofilm matrix.

The lower Ks value for nitrate elimination, compared to COD, shows a greater microbial affinity for the nitrate substrate. This shows that denitrifying bacteria were able to consume nitrate efficiently even at relatively low substrate concentrations. Additionally, the decreased Ks indicates that nitrate uptake was very efficient in substrate-limited conditions and that the microbial population responded well to nitrate reduction29. Similar results have been demonstrated in denitrifying biofilm reactors, where nitrate Ks values normally range from 5 to 20 mg/L depending on reactor hydrodynamics and carbon availability18,20.

The increase in growth rate during the first substrate concentration range and the steady-state approach to saturation at increasing substrate concentration are validated by Monod plots. The approach of the saturation constant is independent of microbial activity, and such limited growth system behaviour is exhibited by the Monod system. Substrate availability strictly controlled microbial growth at lower concentrations, and the growth rate approached the maximum metabolic activity of the attached biomass at higher concentrations30. The flat curve approach of the curves confirms the absence of substrate inhibition as concentration is increased, and viewing reactor efficiency consistency throughout the simultaneous removal of COD and nitrate.

A strong link relationship is established between dilution rate, biomass distribution, mass transfer characteristics, and substrate consumption kinetics for the overall hydrodynamic behaviour of the DTSBBR. The importance of reactor hydrodynamics in regulating the effectiveness of simultaneous COD and nitrate removal is well demonstrated by the decrease in biofilm thickness and the corresponding increase in biomass as dilution rate is increased, supporting the kinetics31. Hence, the combination of hydrodynamics and Monod kinetics is important to create full-scale DTSBBR systems and scale-up correlations. The feasibility of the reactor for simultaneous removal of COD and nitrate applications is also confirmed by the obtained kinetic coefficients and the strong R2 values of the Monod plots. The growth process showed steady microbial retention, with substrate utilisation efficiency increasing along with good hydrodynamic mixing, which encourages the transport of substrate to the biofilm surface. These kinetic parameters greatly benefit reactor process optimisation and modelling for further scale-up research.

sec.title: Empirical model for mass transfer coefficient with dimensionless number correlations
sec.p: The biofilm and hydrodynamic parameters obtained from the experiments were used to perform an empirical mass transfer analysis and quantitatively assess the transport characteristics governing simultaneous COD and nitrate removal in the Draft Tube Spouted Bed Bioreactor (DTSBBR). The equations presented in 2.4 were applied to the experimental data with different GAC loading and dilution rates to obtain the mass transfer correlations. As COD and nitrate have distinct molecular diffusivities, microbial utilisation rates, and concentration gradients across the liquid boundary layer, the external mass transfer coefficient for each substrate was calculated independently. As a result, distinct Sherwood-Reynolds-Schmidt correlations were created for every substrate to precisely depict their unique transport properties as presented in Tables 1 and 2. The obtained empirical models allow for the prediction of substrate-specific mass transfer behaviour and offer practical design equations for the optimisation and scaling up of DTSBBRs that treat wastewaters that contain both carbon and nitrogen.

The DTSBBR demonstrated increased transport efficiency for COD while retaining effective simultaneous nitrate removal by successfully combining hydrodynamic enhancement with biofilm-mediated reactions.

sec.p: The simultaneous removal of nitrate and COD in the spouted bed reactor showed that the substrate removal efficiency was determined by a combination of external mass transfer, biofilm properties, and reactor hydrodynamics. The external mass transfer tests showed that substrate transport through the biofilm-coated granular activated carbon (GAC) particles and liquid-film diffusion had a significant impact on both COD oxidation and nitrate denitrification. According to the experimental findings for COD and Nitrate as tabulated in Tables 1 and 2, raising the dilution rate from 0.6 to 1.2/h changed the reactor’s hydrodynamic behaviour, which had an impact on the mass transfer coefficients, biofilm thickness, effectiveness factor, and Thiele modulus. These factors had a major impact on the reactor system’s biodegradation performance and substrate consumption efficiency.

For both COD and nitrate systems, biofilm thickness gradually decreased as the dilution rate and GAC loading increased. The biofilm thickness decreased from 8.10 to 5.56 μm in the COD removal trials, and comparable decreases were noted for nitrate removal. Increased shear stress and particle mobility produced at greater fluid velocities within the spouted bed reactor are responsible for this decrease. The enhanced circulation during hydrodynamics inhibited excessive biomass buildup on the GAC surface32. Thin biofilms reduce microbial retention and activity and reduce internal diffusion resistance33. Balanced biofilm growth that sustained both substrate and microbial activity simultaneously was observed during reactor operation. Similar results have been reported in fluidised biofilm reactors, where increased turbulence limits uncontrolled biofilm growth and improves substrate accessibility to the microbial layer34–36.

The Thiele modulus values for COD and nitrate removal provided more evidence of the effect of internal diffusion restrictions on reactor performance. The Thiele modulus dropped from 1.98 to 1.60 for COD removal and from 1.72 to 1.41 for nitrate removal as the dilution rate increased. A drop in Thiele modulus indicates reduced internal substrate diffusion resistance within the biofilm matrix. Reduced Thiele modulus values indicate that microbial consumption efficiency increased as the substrate diffusion rate approached the intrinsic biodegradation rate37.

As a result, both systems’ efficacy factors slightly rose, indicating improved substrate consumption within the biofilm-coated particles. While nitrate removal showed values between 0.081 and 0.099, the COD efficacy factor rose from 0.071 to 0.090. Despite the slower denitrification kinetics, the somewhat greater efficiency factor for nitrate indicates comparatively better substrate penetration inside the thinner denitrifying biofilm20,38.

The computed effectiveness factor (η = 0.071–0.099) and Thiele modulus (Φ = 1.42–1.98) show that significant internal diffusion resistance affected substrate transport inside the biofilm. Substratum diffusion and microbial reaction happened simultaneously since Φ was greater than unity under all operating circumstances, suggesting a mixed diffusion–reaction regime rather than only kinetic control. Because substrate concentrations gradually dropped from the biofilm surface toward the inside, the comparatively low efficiency factor indicates that only a portion of the immobilized biomass was fully used. Such behaviour is typical of immobilized biofilm reactors and does not always mean that the reactor is operating poorly. The DTSBBR successfully accomplished simultaneous COD oxidation and nitrate reduction in spite of these internal diffusion limitations because of enhanced exterior mass transfer produced by continuous spouting and liquid circulation. These results also imply that biofilm thickness, particle diameter, superficial liquid velocity, or carrier characteristics could be optimized to minimize internal diffusion resistance while maintaining biofilm stability in order to improve reactor performance in the future.

The observed reaction rates and external mass transfer coefficients showed significant distinctions between the nitrate reduction and COD oxidation processes. Under the same operating circumstances, COD removal showed bigger mass transfer coefficients and higher reported reaction rates than nitrate removal. As dilution rate and GAC loading increased, the measured COD response rate dropped from 2.133 to 1.978, while nitrate removal rates dropped from 1.022 to 0.911.

Similarly, nitrate showed somewhat lower values between 0.66 × 10− 6 and 0.94 × 10− 6 m/s, but the external mass transfer coefficient for COD ranged from 0.73 × 10− 6 to 1.04 × 10− 6 m/s. These results clearly demonstrate that COD biodegradation and transport happened more rapidly than nitrate denitrification. Organic compounds contained in COD are usually more readily biodegradable and transported toward the biofilm surface than nitrate ions, which undergo many enzyme reduction processes during denitrification and nitrate elimination remained relatively slower39.

The dimensionless numbers were evaluated with the hydrodynamic characteristics of the reactor. As the dilution rate increased, the Reynolds number increased from 3.75 to 7.50, indicating improved liquid circulation and particle movement inside the reactor. Although the Reynolds number is in the low flow domain, the improved fluid velocity supported substrate transport and mixing of biofilm-coated particles. As the fluid properties and molecular diffusivity were the same throughout the reactor and all the studies, the Schmidt number remained at 1227. This high Schmidt number is due to diffusion-controlled transport behaviour within the reactor system, where momentum diffusion was subordinate to molecular diffusion resistance.

The mass transfer efficiency was evaluated by the Sherwood number, which varied from 5.10 to 7.10 for COD removal and 4.60 to 6.42 for nitrate removal. The high range of COD numbers shows that external substrate transfer is better and more efficient than diffusion over the liquid boundary surrounding the biofilm particles, and conversely for the slower transport towards the nitrate removal range of numbers. Higher liquid velocities improved convective mass transfer by decreasing the thickness of the external hydrodynamic boundary layer around the biofilm-coated GAC particles, as seen by the Sherwood number increasing with the dilution rate. Despite the decrease in hydraulic retention time, the increased turbulence encouraged more substrate transport from the bulk liquid to the biofilm surface, enhancing the external mass transfer efficiency.

The empirical mass transfer correlations were created to link substrate transfer behaviour to hydrodynamic and diffusion phenomena, as shown in Table 3 for the removal of COD and nitrate. The higher Reynolds number facilitated diffusion towards the biofilm surface, enhancing hydrodynamic mixing and decreasing the external boundary layer40. The higher Reynolds number component for nitrate transfer or the denitrification process was more susceptible to hydrodynamic augmentation and reactor mixing settings.

The Schmidt number exponent of 0.33 found for both correlations is frequently reported for liquid-film diffusion-controlled systems, and this strongly demonstrates that external diffusion mechanisms dominated substrate transport in the spouted bed reactor. The higher coefficient for COD (0.83) compared to nitrate (0.76) indicates stronger intrinsic substrate transfer capability and more effective biodegradation kinetics, reflecting slower biological denitrification reactions. Hydrodynamic mixing, external liquid-film diffusion, and biofilm-facilitated biodegradation mechanisms all highlight the mass-transfer studies for concurrent removal of COD and nitrate. The results showed faster COD removal than nitrate removal, as diffusion-limited denitrification processes slowed nitrate removal, whereas COD removal increased due to rapid oxidation kinetics and efficient substrate use. Table 4 presents a comparison of COD and nitrate removal in a spouted bed bioreactor. The derived empirical correlations successfully depicted the influence of Reynolds number and Schmidt number on substrate transport behaviour for the purpose of scaling up and developing spouted bed biofilm reactors for the simultaneous removal of organic matter and nitrogen from wastewater systems.

The developed correlations have provided predictive equations for determining the external mass transfer coefficients. The empirical correlations found here can be directly applied to process optimisation, reactor design, and scale-up from the standpoint of waste engineering. The correlations reduce design uncertainty and operating costs by allowing the prediction of external mass transfer coefficients from easily observable hydrodynamic parameters without the need for costly pilot-scale experiments. Moreover, a thorough prediction framework for continuous biofilm reactor design is established by combining biofilm characteristics, dimensionless analysis, and Monod kinetic parameters. These results show that, to achieve consistent reactor performance, hydrodynamic parameters and carrier loading adjustment are just as crucial as microbial kinetics. Therefore, for the development of large-scale DTSBBR that contain nitrate and mixed organic carbon pollutants, the proposed empirical model is a helpful engineering tool for engineering design and first scale-up within comparable operating regimes. The methodology can be extended to other biofilm-based wastewater treatment systems. It also serves as a basis for upcoming computational fluid dynamics (CFD)-based optimisation and industrial-scale validation.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: The effectiveness and feasibility of the reactor DTSBBR, through integrated kinetic, mass transfer and hydrodynamic studies, was demonstrated for the simultaneous removal of COD and Nitrate. The reactor, under different conditions of dilution rate and GAC loading, and with its potential advancement in biological treatment systems, showed stable biofilm growth and efficient pollutant removal. The increased dilution rate enhanced liquid circulation and particle movement, which in turn resulted in better substrate transport and minimised diffusion limitations within the biofilm. The microbial utilisation efficiency was well demonstrated by reduced biofilm thickness and Thiele modulus, and an increase in the effectiveness factor. The higher COD reduction was supported by the mass transfer analysis, with higher external mass transfer coefficients and Sherwood numbers than for nitrate reduction, indicating faster transport of organic substrates. The slower nitrate reduction was controlled by denitrification kinetics. The reactor hydrodynamics confirmed that both processes were predominantly governed by the liquid-film diffusion mechanism and by the developed empirical correlations: Sh = 0.83 Re 0.52 Sc 0.33 for COD and Sh = 0.76 Re 0.50 Sc 0.33 for nitrate. The maximum specific growth rates of 0.25/h for COD and 0.23/h for nitrate, and constants Ks of 25 and 14 mg/L, respectively, demonstrated the Monod kinetics. Hence, the results obtained strongly indicate rapid COD removal and strong nitrate removal because of microbial affinity, validating the suitability of the DTSBBR for simultaneous carbon and nitrogen removal. The novelty of the work combines external mass transfer analysis, hydrodynamic characterisation, and Monod kinetics into a single DTSBBR system for the simultaneous removal of nitrate and COD. Additionally, in order to offer quantifiable design parameters for reactor optimization and scale-up, empirical Sherwood number correlations were constructed under various operating situations.
